questions.q: In this course's convention, how is the Discrete Fourier Transform defined?
options: X_k is only defined when N is a power of 2
X_k = the maximum value among all x_j, regardless of k
X_k = Sum over j of x_j times e^(2*pi*i*jk/N) — the positive-exponent convention, chosen to match the Quantum Fourier Transform's convention used later in this chapter
X_k = x_k squared, with no sum over j at all
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly adopts the positive-exponent sign convention so that it matches the QFT's convention introduced in Lesson 6, avoiding any sign-translation step between the two lessons.

questions.q: Why is the DFT described as a 'change of basis'?
options: It re-expresses the same information -- a sequence of N numbers -- in a different but equivalent form (frequency components instead of values at each position), with no information lost and the transform invertible
It converts complex numbers into real numbers so they are easier to store
It permanently deletes half of the information in the original sequence
It only works on sequences that are already sorted in increasing order
questions.explain: The DFT doesn't destroy or add information -- it re-describes the exact same sequence from the 'value at each position' viewpoint to the 'how much of each frequency' viewpoint, and the transform can always be inverted.

questions.q: In the worked 4x4 DFT matrix given in the lesson, row k=0 is [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5]. What does this row represent?
options: The row that corresponds to the input vector itself, unchanged
The highest possible frequency representable by a length-4 sequence
Frequency 0, the 'DC' or average component -- every input contributes equally with no phase difference, which is why e^(2*pi*i*0*j/4) = 1 for every j
An error in the matrix, since all rows should contain complex numbers
questions.explain: When k=0, the exponent 2*pi*i*0*j/N is always 0 for any j, so e^0 = 1 for every entry -- row 0 is always constant at 1/sqrt(N) in every column, regardless of N, representing the zero-frequency (average) component.

questions.q: Why does the naive method of computing a DFT directly from its formula take O(N^2) time?
options: Because every DFT must be computed twice to check for errors
Computing each of the N output values requires summing N terms, so N outputs times N terms per output gives N times N = O(N^2) total multiplications
O(N^2) is simply a historical convention with no connection to the actual arithmetic required
Because the DFT formula involves a nested loop over all pairs of complex numbers in the universe
questions.explain: Reading the formula directly, each of the N outputs X_k is a sum over all N inputs x_j, so the direct computation costs N times N = O(N^2) multiplications total.

questions.q: What does the classical Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm actually change compared to the naive O(N^2) approach?
options: It is a quantum algorithm that requires a quantum computer to run
It only works for sequences where every value is zero
It computes a different, approximate transform that sacrifices some accuracy for speed
It computes the mathematically identical DFT output, just restructured to exploit repeating structure in the roots of unity, reducing the runtime to O(N log N) with no quantum computer involved
questions.explain: The FFT produces the exact same DFT result as the naive method, just faster -- O(N log N) instead of O(N^2) -- by recursively exploiting structure in the roots of unity. It is entirely classical, which matters for contrasting against the QFT in Lesson 8.
